title: Boniface and the oak
hookLine: an English monk fells a sacred oak in Germany and the mission grows; he's martyred in 754
tomorrow: John of Damascus and the icons

cards: A huge old oak stands at a place called Geismar, in the land of Hesse. People gather there and honor the tree as holy, the dwelling of a god.
One day a bishop from England, a monk by training, walks up to it with an axe, while a crowd watches and, the story says, curses him under its breath. He begins to cut.
The question hangs in the air: if this tree belongs to a god, what happens to the man who strikes it? Today, Boniface and the oak.

teach.b: Our account comes from Willibald, a priest who wrote the life of Boniface from what his companions told him.
Boniface was born in England, became a monk, and chose to leave home to preach among the peoples east of the Rhine; by the time of the oak, Willibald says, the pope had made him a bishop.
Some people in Hesse, Willibald says, had been baptized but still honored the old sacred places, and one of those was a great oak. Boniface and his companions began to cut it down.

teach.h: A WIND, AND THE TREE BREAKS.
teach.b: After only a little cutting, a great wind shook the tree, and it crashed to the ground and broke into four pieces. The people who had cursed him stopped cursing and began to bless God.

Boniface used the timber to build a small chapel, dedicated to Saint Peter. The wood of the old worship became the walls of the new. Willibald tells this as a victory, and that is how the story has been handed down.
Some readers today also feel the loss: a tree people loved, cut down in front of them.
Both can be held. It's a story of one man's courage, and of a people's old faith giving way. His mission grew; he organized churches and monasteries in Germany.
Years later, Willibald says, in Frisia, he was killed by attackers while waiting to confirm new Christians, and he told his companions not to fight back. Catholics honor him as a saint and martyr.
And the moment the crowd stopped breathing: the oak fell.

how: The Catholic Church keeps the feast of Saint Boniface, bishop and martyr, and churches in Germany are dedicated to him; the oak of Geismar is told as part of his story.

s: Willibald's life says Boniface set up the first Christmas tree
that's a later legend. Willibald tells of the oak falling and a chapel built from its wood.
the chapel built from the oak was dedicated to Saint Peter
Willibald says Boniface used the timber for a chapel to Saint Peter.
Boniface told his companions to fight back when attacked
Willibald says he told them not to fight.

games.q: you're Boniface. people who were baptized still honor a sacred oak, and a crowd is watching. what do you do?
o: leave the tree alone and keep preaching.
cut the oak down in front of everyone.
go somewhere the old faith isn't so strong.
games.why: he cut it. Willibald says a wind brought it down, it broke in pieces, and Boniface built a chapel from the wood.

practice: In the Bible's language, an idol is something given more trust than it can bear: a phone checked every few minutes, a number in a bank account, someone's approval.
Breathe, and ask yourself gently what has grown too tall in your life; don't cut it down in anger, just name it and notice the hold it has. If you pray, hand that hold to God for these two minutes.

wordCard.voice: Boniface. An English monk cuts down a sacred tree in Hesse, it falls and breaks, and he builds a chapel from its wood. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the oak of Jupiter — Willibald's name for the tree, using a Roman god's name for a Germanic one.

carryVoice: Your line: the oak fell. Courage and loss, both inside one story. Day seven hundred fifty-nine, done.
